title: After Trumpâ€™s move, White House says Biden to speak on Jan 6
text: President Joe Biden will make a public statement on the anniversary of the January 6 riot at the US Capitol, the White House said. This comes after former President Donald Trump said he would hold a public event on that day. â€œI think it's safe to say that the American people will hear from him on that day,â€ White House Press Secretary Jen Psaki said at a news briefing on Wednesday, when asked if Biden would speak. Psaki said last week that Biden wanted to commemorate â€œone of the darkest days in our democracy,â€ but could give no details at that point as to what specifically he might do. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-California) said on Monday she was planning a â€œsolemn observanceâ€ of the anniversary, featuring a panel of historians, a â€œprayerful vigil,â€ and an opportunity for members of Congress to â€œshare their experiences and reflections from that day,â€ even though the House is not scheduled to be in session. On Tuesday, Trump said he would hold a news conference at his residence, the Mar-a-Lago Club, in Florida, to address what he called a protest against the â€œrigged election.â€ While the Democrats have called the January 6 events an â€œinsurrection,â€ Trump said the actual insurrection â€œtook place on November 3,â€ the 2020 election day. On January 6, the House of Representatives and the Senate met in a joint session to certify the 2020 election results, according to which Biden won the presidency. Trump alleged irregularities and fraud, giving a speech outside the White House earlier in the day. After a group of people urged his supporters to storm the Capitol, hundreds of people entered the building and disrupted Congress just as Republicans began objecting to the election results. Four of the protesters died in the ensuing riot â€“ one of them fatally shot by a Capitol Police officer. When Congress reconvened later that evening, Republicans dropped their objections to the election results amid Democrat accusations of â€œinsurrection.â€ None of the participants in the riot have been charged with insurrection, which is a specific term in the 14th Amendment â€“ adopted after the Civil War â€“ under which those declared rebels against the government can be stripped of citizenship and voting rights.

title: Trump reveals why he didnâ€™t pardon Snowden or Assange
text: Former President Donald Trump has said he was â€œvery close to going the other wayâ€ on issuing a pardon for Julian Assange or Edward Snowden before he left the White House, ultimately deciding not to grant clemency to either. During an interview with the Daily Wireâ€™s Candace Owens this week, Trump was asked why he failed to issue pardons to WikiLeaks co-founder Assange and National Security Agency (NSA) whistleblower Snowden, which activists had been pushing for in the presidentâ€™s final months in office. â€œYou have two sides of it,â€ Trump said. He described their separate situations as, respectively, a â€œsort of a spy deal going onâ€ and â€œsomebody thatâ€™s exposing real corruption,â€ but without indicating which description applied to which person, concluding only that he felt â€œa little bit more strongly about one than the other.â€ Media reports earlier this year indicated Trump had been convinced by aides that an Assange or a Snowden pardon would upset Senate Republicans, who were gearing up to vote in his impeachment trial at the time. He also appeared to negatively reference Assange and â€œspyingâ€ at one point, though he did not elaborate. â€œThere [were] some spying things, and there [were] some bad things released that really set us back and really hurt us with what they did,â€ he said, according to the Daily Wire. It was alleged during the opening stages of Assangeâ€™s extradition hearing in London last year that the journalist had been offered a pardon in exchange for spinning the origin of hacked Democratic emails sent during the 2016 presidential campaign. The White House denied the claim and said the president â€œbarelyâ€ knew the Republican congressman through which the deal had allegedly been offered. The congressman, in turn, said he had made the proposal on his own initiative and the White House had not endorsed it. Trump said he had ultimately decided to let the issue be handled in the courtroom. â€œI guess the courts are actually doing that,â€ he said. Trump explains to Candace Owens why he started the prosecution of Assange and didn't pardon Assange/Snowden. pic.twitter.com/EknNzx4A4n Assange is currently being held in a UK prison, from where it was recently ruled he can be extradited to the US to stand trial on espionage charges for having published documents related to alleged US war crimes during the Afghanistan and Iraq campaigns. He faces up to 175 years in prison if convicted. His mental and physical health has deteriorated during his 20 months of incarceration, and he recently suffered a stroke. Snowden, who has remained a fugitive from the US since whistleblowing on the NSA for unconstitutional spying on the American public in 2013, seemed a more likely candidate for a presidential pardon. The former president said last year he was â€œlookingâ€ at Snowdenâ€™s case, noting that many felt he had â€œnot been treated fairly.â€ This about-face surprised many commentators, given that Trump had previously referred to the former NSA contractor as a â€œspy who should be executed.â€

title: Military medics tout new vaccine to end Covid-19 pandemic
text: A candidate vaccine that uses a novel platform and may be good enough to deal with existing and emerging variants of SARS-CoV-2 viruses, will reportedly be announced soon by researchers at the Walter Reed Army Institute in the US. The unveiling may come â€œwithin weeks,â€ according to Dr. Kayvon Modjarrad, director of Walter Reedâ€™s infectious diseases branch, who was interviewed by Defense One. According to the military publication, the candidate vaccine may offer a single-shot, wide-scale immunity from diseases caused by human coronaviruses, including from future mutations. The formula uses a novel Spike Ferritin Nanoparticle (SpFN) platform. Ferritins are natural proteins shaped like globular cages that are normally used by an organism to store iron. Its self-assembly properties have made it an interesting tool for nanofabrication applications. In the case of vaccination, the proteinâ€™s 24 subunits can be fitted with protein spikes similar to those that viruses use to attach to living cells before infecting them. Such nanoparticles may be injected to train the immune system to fight against real viruses. With various kinds of spike proteins included in the same vaccine, it can immunize against a wide range of viruses, past and future, the researchers hope. Modjarradâ€™s team says it has good expectations about the efficacy and other properties of their SpFN vaccine-in-waiting, after conducting clinical trials with animals. Their latest publication in Science Translational Medicine details experiments they conducted on rhesus macaques. A separate, Phase 1 human trial has been underway since April. The challenge with the human trials, Modjarrad told Defense One, was and remains finding people who are still unvaccinated and never caught Covid-19 for the studies to be accurate. He added that his team also wants to evaluate their product â€œin the real-world settingâ€ with people who were vaccinated or whoâ€™ve recovered from the disease.

title: Biden claims â€˜almost allâ€™ Covid victims in America were unvaccinated
text: Claiming that â€œalmost allâ€ of over 400,000 Americans who died of Covid-19 in 2021 were unvaccinated, US President Joe Biden demanded everyone get vaccinated and boosted as a â€œpatriotic dutyâ€ amid the spread of the Omicron variant. â€œWe should all be concerned about Omicron, but not panicked. If youâ€™re fully vaccinated, especially if you got your booster shot, youâ€™re highly protected,â€ Biden told reporters at the White House on Tuesday afternoon. â€œAlmost everyone who has died of Covid-19 over the past many months has been unvaccinated,â€ he said, adding that those who got the vaccines and boosters have a â€œhigh degree of protection against severe illness.â€ Biden urged Americans to get vaccinated if they havenâ€™t already, and get booster shots if they have, so they can safely celebrate Christmas and the upcoming holidays. Everyone still ought to wear a mask in indoor public settings, the president added. BIDEN: "If you're not fully vaccinated, you have good reason to be concerned...You're at a high risk of getting sick...Almost everyone who has died from COVID-19 in the past many months has been unvaccinated" pic.twitter.com/erDV7sLQuT Repeating that â€œalmost allâ€ Americans who died of the virus were unvaccinated, Biden insisted his vaccination mandates were put in place â€œnot to control your life, but to save your life, and the lives of others.â€ 400,000 of Americans died from Covid this calendar year, and almost all were unvaccinated, almost all were preventable. In addition to the mandate, which he said was just upheld by courts, Biden said the White House was dipping into emergency management funding to deploy 10,000 more vaccination sites and pop-up clinics for boosters, as well as having FEMA send additional ambulances and build overflow hospitals in New York and Maine, where infections are rising the fastest. Time and again, Biden blamed the â€œunvaccinatedâ€ for dying, infecting others, and causing hospitals to be overwhelmed. Their choice not to take the jab is â€œfueled by dangerous misinformation on TV and social media,â€ he argued, calling it â€œwrongâ€ and â€œimmoralâ€ and shouting that people doing this need to â€œstop it now.â€ After his presentation, Biden turned to the White House press corps and answered several questions, before saying â€œIâ€™m not supposed to be having this press conference right now.â€ He did answer a follow-up question about Senator Joe Manchin (D-West Virginia), then walked away.

title: Biden staffer tests positive for Covid
text: An aide to US President Joe Biden has tested positive for Covid-19 after spending time with the commander in chief days prior, the White House has confirmed, though Biden will continue his usual duties and forego quarantine. title: Trump sues NY attorney general

title: Pentagonâ€™s new extremism rules extend to â€˜likesâ€™ â€“ reports
text: The US military has updated its â€œextremismâ€ policy, allowing commanders to punish service members for â€œactively participatingâ€ in banned activities â€“ from supporting terrorism to liking a post deemed extremist on social media. The new rules were rolled out on Monday, Department of Defense officials told AP, though the official document has not been made publicly available yet. It is the first update to the extremism policy since 2012. The update focuses â€œexclusively on actionsâ€ as opposed to â€œany particular ideology or any political organization,â€ one DOD official told reporters at a background briefing. That means the prohibition on â€œparticipationâ€ in groups that advocate any kind of â€œsupremacist, extremist, or criminal gang doctrine, ideology, or causesâ€ remains in effect, as well as groups that â€œadvocate the use of force, violence, or criminal activity; or otherwise engage in efforts to deprive individuals of their civil rights.â€ Whatâ€™s new is the definition of six broad categories of â€œextremist activitiesâ€ and 14 definitions of what constitutes â€œactive participationâ€ in them. Under the new rules, a commander can penalize a service member if they actively participated in behavior that fits the definition of extremism. As reported by AP, among the banned activities are advocating terrorism and supporting the overthrow of the government, fundraising and rallying on behalf of groups designated as extremist, and liking or reposting such views on social media. In February, Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin ordered a one-day â€œstand downâ€ of the entire military to address â€œextremismâ€ in the ranks in the wake of the January 6 riot at the US Capitol. Fewer than 100 service members were involved in â€œsubstantiated cases of extremist activityâ€ over the past year, officials told AP on Monday, but added that the Pentagon fears that number may grow, particularly among veterans. title: Donald Trump Jr. explains why Chinaâ€™s not intimidated by US military
text: Donald Trumpâ€™s eldest son has claimed Beijing is far from being intimidated by the US military, pointing, as evidence, to the air serviceâ€™s latest guidelines on the equal treatment of transgender personnel. title: Biden pushes â€˜aggressiveâ€™ green mileage standard
text: The Biden administration is citing climate change to drastically raise the vehicle mileage standard to 55 miles per gallon by 2026. The White House expects this to result in doubling of electric vehicle sales in the coming years. The rule, announced Monday, will see the standard raised to 40 mpg in 2023 and up every year from there. The rule was â€œa giant step forwardâ€ in delivering on President Joe Bidenâ€™s agenda to combat climate change, he added, â€œwhile paving the way toward an all-electric, zero-emissions transportation future.â€ According to the EPA, the rule will help slow climate change, improve public health, and lower the cost of driving through improved fuel efficiency. The agency estimates it will lower the consumption of gasoline by about 360 billion tons, prevent the release of 3.1 million tons of carbon dioxide through 2050, and save drivers about $1,080 over the lifetime of their new vehicle. The new standard would also help drive the sales of zero-emissions vehicles such as plug-in hybrids and electric cars, which are expected to have about 7% of the US market share in 2023. The Biden administration wants to see that reach 17% by 2026. The new rules will start applying to 2023 vehicle models and ratchet up the emissions standard every year through 2026, much faster than previous rules. The EPA believes carmakers can meet the target by rolling out more electric vehicles. â€œMaking cars cleaner is critical to address climate change,â€ the agency said. Some former Obama administration officials think the rule doesnâ€™t go far enough. It is â€œbasically just recapturing the emissions cuts that we lost during the Trump rollback,â€ former EPA policy adviser Jeff Alson told the New York Times. â€œThatâ€™s good, but itâ€™s not going to get us anywhere near the level weâ€™ve got to get to reduce vehicle emissions enough to protect the planet.â€ Dan Becker of the Safe Climate Transport Campaign at the Center for Biological Diversity said the rule isnâ€™t up to addressing the â€œexistential threatâ€ of global warming. â€œWhat we really need is an aggressive rule as soon as possible to phase out the gasoline-powered vehicles that are guzzling and polluting, and replace them with EVs that have no tailpipe,â€ he said. Transportation accounts for 29% of US greenhouse gas emissions, according to AP. Trucks and passenger cars account for 58% of transportation-related emissions. The rule will affect almost all Americans, as there were over 286 million registered cars in the US as of 2020, and more than 72% of all freight in the country is transported by trucks, according to industry estimates.

title: US Navy vessels fired on mystery drone swarms â€“ media
text: United States Navy vessels were forced to fire on unidentified drones off the coast of Southern California after they were swarmed by mystery UAVs in 2019, according to documents obtained by The Drive. Throughout July 2019, the US Navy was reportedly plagued by mystery drone swarms that harassed vessels in the Channel Islands archipelago near California, according to ship log documents released through a Freedom of Information (FOI) request. Two days later, to protect the USS Russell, US naval officials deployed whatâ€™s called a â€˜ghostbustersâ€™ team, which counters unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) by jamming radio frequencies.10 days after the initial incident, the USS Russellâ€™s ships log, which was heavily redacted, showed another swarm terrorized the vessel, forcing another â€˜ghostbustersâ€™ team to be deployed to the region in the early hours of the morning. title: Retired generals warn of â€˜lethal chaosâ€™ in US military after 2024 vote

title: Texas restarts Trumpâ€™s pet project
text: Texas has begun building a wall on its border with Mexico, picking up where former President Donald Trump left off with the stated goal of stopping the trafficking of drugs and illegal aliens through its territory. Governor Greg Abbott announced the start of construction on Saturday, saying crews are already putting up more than 100 yards of wall â€“ made with the same 30-foot steel poles the Trump administration was using â€“ each day. He noted that the state had made â€œunprecedentedâ€ progress in pushing forward with building work just six months after he announced the project. â€œWe have wasted no time in the six months since that promise was made...â€ Abbott said. â€œToday not only represents the first phase of the Texas border wall, but it also serves as a major milestone in our efforts to combat illegal immigration, stop the smuggling of drugs and people, and keep our communities safe.â€ The wall is part of a $3 billion initiative that Abbott launched in June to address the effects of a US immigration crisis on Texas, where about two-thirds of illegal crossings at the southern border occur. title: Retiring NIH director issues warning to â€˜tiredâ€™ Americans
text: National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director Francis Collins has called holiday travel for unvaccinated Americans â€œnot a great ideaâ€ and left a dire warning about Omicron cases in his final days on the job. title: Trump says he had â€˜a great relationshipâ€™ with â€˜killerâ€™ Xi

title: NYT investigation reveals â€˜hundredsâ€™ of civilian deaths uncounted in US strikes
text: An investigation by the New York Times has found that the Pentagon severely downplayed the civilian death toll from its â€œprecisionâ€ strikes in Syria and Iraq, while failing to investigate reports of potential civilian casualties. The New York Times investigation, the first part of which was released on Monday, draws on over 1,311 casualty assessment reports that were previously kept under wraps by the Pentagon. Having reviewed the files and visited â€œnearly 100 casualties sitesâ€ in Iraq, Syria, and Afghanistan, the Times reported that the US military often dismissed reports of civilian casualties as non-credible, despite failing to visit the sites or speak to the witnesses. The Times revealed that in 216 instances in which the Pentagon found reports of civilian casualties credible, its investigators visited the actual site of the bombing in only one case. None of the investigations resulted in any penalties for those responsible for the strikes, and only one â€œpossible violationâ€ in mapping out a strike was identified by the Pentagon. The Times investigation also revealed that trigger-happy US troops tended to rely on â€œincorrect or incompleteâ€ intelligence to hit terrorist targets, sometimes killing dozens of civilians instead. Confirmation bias was said to play a role in troops interpreting scant intelligence in a way that affirms their â€œpre-existing beliefsâ€ about the targets. For instance, during a strike in Iraq in 2015, US forces killed a child after identifying him as â€œan unknown heavy objectâ€ who was being â€œdraggedâ€ to a supposed Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS) position by an alleged militant. Sloppy targeting practices resulted in around 120 Syrian villagers dying in a US strike on July 19, 2016, according to the investigation. At the time of the strike, the Pentagon apparently thought that 85 militants were killed in the bombing instead, even though it took place â€œfar from the front line.â€ In another botched strike, a warplane killed an entire family escaping West Mosul in 2017, mistaking the civilian vehicle with two children for a car bomb. Even in instances in which the US acknowledged civilian casualties, it was not in a hurry to pay compensation to the victims, with the Times reporting that â€œfewer than a dozen condolence payments were made.â€ The Times points out that the multiple lapses in the US air campaign cannot be discounted as â€œoutliers,â€ but rather represent a common trend in â€œa sharp contrast to the American governmentâ€™s image of war waged by all-seeing drones and precision bombs.â€ â€œSince 2014, the American air war has been plagued by deeply flawed intelligence, rushed and imprecise targeting and the deaths of thousands of civilians, many of them children.â€ While the Pentagon claims that a total of 1,417 civilians died as result of the US bombing campaigns in Syria and Iraq, and 188 civilians were killed since 2018 in Afghanistan, the Times estimates the civilian death toll to be significantly higher. â€œMany allegations of civilian casualties had been summarily discounted, with scant evaluation. And the on-the-ground reporting â€“ involving a sampling of cases dismissed, cases deemed â€˜credibleâ€™ and, in Afghanistan, cases not included in the trove of Pentagon documents â€“ found hundreds of deaths uncounted.â€

title: US military causes â€˜sonic boomâ€™ by accident
text: An Air National Guard unit in Oregon has apologized after one of its aircraft â€œinadvertentlyâ€ caused a sonic boom that raised concerns that the state was being rocked by an earthquake. The incident occurred on Tuesday, just a week after Oregon was shaken by a swarm of nearly 100 offshore earthquakes. A day later, the 142nd Wing of the Oregon Air National Guard confessed that it was to blame for the shocking boom. A training flight â€œinadvertently went supersonicâ€ while operating off the Oregon coast, the unit said in a Facebook post. â€œWe understand that this caused concern from our coastal residents and for that we sincerely apologize.â€ Sgt. Steven Conklin said Air National Guard pilots are allowed to cause such booms when flying at least 15 miles away from the coast, but the nose of the aircraft should be pointed away from land. In Tuesdayâ€™s incident, the jet was located more than 15 miles offshore, but its nose was pointed â€œslightly toward the coastline,â€ he said. Sonic booms are triggered by the shock waves that are created when an object travels through the air at faster than the speed of sound, or about 760 miles per hour. The booms sound similar to an explosion and can damage eardrums and shatter windows. The US Air Force and Navy have paid out hundreds of damage and injury claims stemming from sonic booms over the years. In one case that the Air Force settled for $26,000 in 1982, a Tennessee family alleged that the boom killed 61 pigs, knocked out a womanâ€™s dental fillings and picked up a house from its foundation. The woman also claimed to have suffered blurred vision, earaches and dizzy spells for weeks. The Federal Aviation Administration has banned supersonic civilian flight over land since 1973. The Air National Guard unit didnâ€™t identify the type of jet involved in Tuesdayâ€™s incident. Some US military jets can fly at more than double the speed of sound.

title: US hypersonic weapon test fails third time in a row
text: The US military didnâ€™t succeed in conducting a test of a hypersonic missile prototype, with the munition failing to decouple from its carrier aircraft. This is the third failure in a row for the US ARRW hypersonic weapon program. The unsuccessful attempt to test the new missile prototype was made by the US Air Force on Wednesday. The munition failed to leave its carrier aircraft for an unspecified reason, returning safely back to the ground. â€œOn 15 Dec. 2021, the Department of the Air Force attempted a booster test flight of the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon (ARRW) from a B-52 Stratofortress,â€ Air Force Brig. Gen. Heath Collins told The War Zone magazine in a statement. The launch sequence was aborted before release with an unknown issue. The missile will return to the factory and analysis of the telemetry and onboard data will begin immediately. The program will seek to resume flight test as quickly as possible. The ARRW is one of the USâ€™ programs to develop hypersonic weaponry, with the Pentagon hoping it will beat competition from Russia and China. The stated goal of the program is to reach initial operational capability with the missile in September 2022, yet underwhelming testing progress might push that objective further into the future. The new unsuccessful test of the AGM-183A missile is the third failure for the US hypersonic weapons program this year. Two previous tests, conducted back in April and July were also unsuccessful.The April test appeared to be similar to the new flop, with the missile failing to separate from the carrier aircraft. During the second test attempt in July, the missile decoupled from the plane yet its engine failed to ignite, with the projectile plummeting to its doom. The failure was described as a â€˜partial successâ€™ by the US military back then, as the testing team was able to collect some data related to the missileâ€™s launch procedure.

title: Will the real president please stand up? Harris bristles at suggestion Biden isnâ€™t it
text: US Vice President Kamala Harris lashed out at TV host Charlamagne Tha God after he jokingly asked her whether the real leader of the country was President Joe Biden or West Virginia Democratic Senator Joe Manchin. Asked which â€œJoeâ€ was the â€œreal president of this country,â€ Harris insisted at first in a resigned tone, â€œCome on Charlamagne, itâ€™s Joe Biden,â€ talking over his attempted replies â€“ â€œI canâ€™t tell sometimesâ€ â€“ with a torrent of patronizing noâ€™s. WATCH: Kamala staffer tries to shut down interview when Harris is asked if Biden/Manchin is in charge.Then she gets shouty and belligerent and accuses the interviewer of sounding like a Republican (revealing she only expects interviewers to be leftists) pic.twitter.com/pGjmef0adE â€œItâ€™s Joe Biden,â€ she repeated, growing increasingly heated and accusing Charlamagne of â€œtalking like a Republican about asking whether or not heâ€™s presidentâ€ as she lapsed into an increasingly self-congratulatory monologue regarding the pairâ€™s plans for their presidency. Manchin, a thorn in the side of the Democratic Party for his refusal to drop everything and toe the party line, remained unmentioned by the VP, though Charlamagne attempted to derail Harrisâ€™ monologue by asking once more, â€œDo you think Joe Manchin is a problem?â€ He had repeatedly attempted to draw out Harrisâ€™ opinion of Manchin earlier in the show. Harris instead reminded Charlamagne of her name and position, waving her finger condescendingly as if speaking to a child. â€œAnd the reality is that because we are in office, we do the things like the child tax credit which is going to reduce black child poverty by 50%,â€ she said, admitting the administration was â€œon trackâ€ to do that rather than actually accomplishing it. â€œWe do things that are about saying that our Department of Justice is going to do these investigations and require that we end choke holds and have body cameras,â€ she continued, seemingly prizing talk over action. Removing lead from pipes and increasing the â€œdignityâ€ of those who ride public transit were also on the list, as was bringing down prescription drug costs and reducing black maternal mortality rates. While most of the issues remain unaddressed one year into the presidency as the administration has focused on Covid-19 aid and vaccine mandates, the debt ceiling, attempting to slay the filibuster, and other partisan issues, they remain key priorities. Charlamagne managed to rescue the segment from that tangent by praising her for her ferocious, if unrelated, delivery. â€œI just want you to know that Madam Vice President, that Kamala Harris, thatâ€™s the one I like â€¦ thatâ€™s the one Iâ€™d like to see more often out here in these streets.â€ While he later tried to convince Harris to blame the Democratsâ€™ issues on Manchin, she refused to do so, instead blaming the problems on elected officials â€œall overâ€ and even dredged up the specter of the January 6 Capitol riot. Manchinâ€™s refusal to back Democratic voting-rights initiatives, which would require overhauling the filibuster â€“ a legislative move that allows a slim majority to block the passage of a bill â€“ or embrace a massive combination infrastructure-social spending package have rankled his party. He has accused the Democrats of hiding the true costs of the $1.75 trillion package, and pointed out that should the filibuster be dismantled, the consequences if Congress falls back into the hands of the Republican Party would be disastrous. Harris has suffered from plummeting approval ratings as the Biden administration has failed to deliver on many of its promises, leaving the nation mired in inflation and economic catastrophe on top of the ongoing Covid-19 pandemic. A Suffolk University poll last month found just 28% approved of Harrisâ€™ handling of her job, with 51% disapproving. Charlamagne Tha God hosted Biden while he was on the campaign trail last year as the Democrat delivered a now-infamous line declaring that any black voter who had trouble deciding between himself and Trump â€œainâ€™t black.â€ Despite what could have been a show-stopping line, the host was able to keep the conversation moving with admirable poise, later eliciting an apology from Biden.

title: Trump claims Israel had â€˜absolute powerâ€™ over Congress

title: Court reinstates Biden vaccine mandate
text: A US federal appeals court has reinstated the Biden administrationâ€™s Covid-19 vaccination mandate for large private businesses, reversing an injunction by another court last month to pause the vaccine and testing requirement. In its ruling on Friday, the Sixth US Court of Appeals in Cincinnati, Ohio upheld the authority of the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) to enforce the mandate, which it called an â€œimportant stepâ€ in curtailing coronavirus transmission. Vaccination and medical examinations are both tools that OSHA historically employed to contain illness in the workplace, Judge Julia Gibbons wrote in her majority opinion. She said the mandate was therefore â€œnot a novel expansion of OSHAâ€™s powerâ€ but an â€œexisting application of authority to a novel and dangerous worldwide pandemic.â€ The mandate, introduced in November, applied to private businesses with at least 100 employees and would have affected 80 million workers. Under threat of fines, businesses were told to ensure their staff were fully vaccinated by January 4 or have them submit weekly Covid-19 tests in order to work. Unvaccinated workers would also have had to wear masks indoors from December 5. However, the Biden administration was forced to suspend the enforcement of the rules after a court halted the order on November 12, citing â€œgrave statutory and constitutional issues.â€ That ruling described the policy as â€œstaggeringly overboardâ€ and â€œfatally flawed.â€ More than two dozen lawsuits were filed by Republican-led states, industry associations, and individual businesses to fight the mandate. They argued that the OSHA was not authorized to impose such rules and said fines for non-compliance â€“ starting at nearly $14,000 per violation â€“ would hurt businesses. The Cincinnati court said such claims were â€œspeculative.â€ Judge Jane Stranch wrote that the â€œharm to the Government and the public interest outweighs any irreparable injuryâ€ to individuals and businesses. In the lone dissenting opinion, Judge Joan Larsen, a Donald Trump nominee, said Congress had not authorized the OSHA to make this sort of rule and argued that vaccinated workers â€œdo not face â€˜grave dangerâ€™ from working with those who are not vaccinated.â€ The mandate â€“ which was repealed by the Senate earlier this month â€“ will likely face scrutiny from the Supreme Court next.

title: California mayor declares state of emergency to tackle drugs, street pooping
text: San Francisco Mayor London Breed declared a state of emergency in the cityâ€™s Tenderloin neighborhood just days after she announced a war on crime, drugs, and public defecation and the culprits behind them. Breed said on Friday that the situation in the Tenderloin â€œcalls for an emergency responseâ€ and that tough action was necessary â€œto make the Tenderloin a safer, more livable place for the families and children who call the neighborhood home.â€ The mayor delivered a fiery speech on Tuesday, vowing to â€œtake the steps to be more aggressive with law enforcementâ€ and â€œless tolerant of all the bull**** that has destroyed our city.â€ Breed claimed that the Tenderloinâ€™s â€œnasty streetsâ€ had been getting worse and that they were â€œfull of feces and urine that the Department of Public Works is cleaning every single day, but it comes back just a few hours later.â€ â€œItâ€™s time the reign of criminals who are destroying our city to come to an end,â€ Breed said at the time, urging prosecutors to get â€œon boardâ€ with the agenda and make sure repeat offenders are not back on the streets â€œagain and again.â€

title: House Covid committee assigns blame for â€˜botchedâ€™ pandemic response
text: Former US President Donald Trump and his administration undermined Americaâ€™s Covid-19 response for the sake of political gain, a Democrat-led House committee involving some of the ex-presidentâ€™s fiercest opponents said. The Trump administrationâ€™s â€œpersistent political interferenceâ€ is to blame for the botched coronavirus response that has seen more than 800,000 Americans dying from the disease so far, the House Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Crisis said in a report on Friday. It placed the blame for what it called â€œone of the worst failures of leadership in American historyâ€ squarely on the 45th president and his administration. The report published by the Democrat majority on Friday is a year-end review of the lengthy inquiry, which saw the subcommittee reviewing hundreds of thousands of pages of various documents, conducting a dozen interviews with â€œkey officials,â€ and holding 14 hearings and public briefings to supposedly get to the bottom of Americaâ€™s shortcomings in fighting the pandemic. The document focused almost entirely on the â€œfailuresâ€ of the Trump administration, while also naming companies that â€œprofited during the pandemicâ€ at the expense of public health. The list of alleged failures ranges from blocking public briefings of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and sidelining the CDC in finalizing certain Covid-19 health guidance, to pressuring the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) into authorizing â€œineffectiveâ€ treatments like hydroxychloroquine. The ex-president and his administration were also accused of favoring a â€œdangerous herd immunity strategyâ€ and taking steps to limit Covid-19 testing to supposedly conceal the speed with which the virus spread throughout the US. Another allegation directly accused Trump and his administration of â€œneglecting the pandemic responseâ€ to fully focus on his re-election and â€œthe Big Lie that the election results were fraudulent.â€ Republicans denounced the report as a partisan product of a â€œsham subcommitteeâ€ aiming to â€œpoliticize the pandemic.â€ â€œPresident Biden promised to â€˜shut down the virus,â€™ but more Americans have died this year from COVID than the previous year. He promised to follow the science, but he allowed union bosses to dictate policy that tags parents as domestic terrorists and effectively keeps schools shuttered,â€ Rep. Steve Scalise (R-Louisiana), who sits on the panel, said in a statement on Friday. The subcommittee was led by Rep. James Clyburn (D-South Carolina), a prominent Democrat, who accused Trump of attempting to start a â€œrace warâ€ in the wake of the US Capitol riot on January 6. Clyburn was also one of the key supporters of the current president, Joe Biden, whose emotional endorsement during the primaries led to him being branded 'kingmaker' in the race. Other Democrats on the panel are also known to be among Trumpâ€™s most vehement critics, including Maxine Waters of California, Trumpâ€™s â€œlead impeachment managerâ€ Jamie Raskin of Maryland, and active impeachment supporters Bill Foster of Illinois and Carolyn B. Maloney of New York.

title: Biden calls VP â€˜President Harrisâ€™ again

title: â€˜Cyber-mercenariesâ€™ spied on Facebook users
text: Meta has banned accounts linked to seven entities for conducting â€˜surveillance-for-hireâ€™ operations against some 50,000 users. One of the purged firms is the Israeli-run Black Cube, hired by disgraced producer Harvey Weinstein. The US tech giant that owns Facebook and Instagram, among other services, says it has busted massive surveillance operations that violated its terms of use. They used Meta platforms to passively spy on users, engage them directly to trick them into revealing sensitive information, and plant malware on their devices, the company reported on Thursday. The seven entities are just part of a burgeoning â€œsurveillance-for-hireâ€ industry brought to life by the connectivity of social media, the company said. Such firms conduct â€œindiscriminate surveillanceâ€ on behalf of their clients, targeting dissidents, journalists, human rights activists and others, it said. Identified after a â€œmonths-long investigation,â€ the seven now-banned actors operated in over 100 countries and targeted around 50,000 people. Meta said it will alert people affected. â€œTo help disrupt these activities, we blocked related infrastructure, banned these entities from our platform and issued Cease and Desist warnings,â€ Meta said. â€œWe also shared our findings with security researchers, other platforms, and policymakers so they too can take appropriate action.â€ Six of the targets for Metaâ€™s punitive action were identified as private security firms: Cobwebs Technologies, Cognyte, Black Cube, Bluehawk CI, BellTroX and Cytrox. Hundreds of accounts linked to each of them were blocked, the company said. As he was presenting Metaâ€™s findings, security chief Nathaniel Gleicher also brought attention to a recent investigation by Citizen Lab, which accused the previously little-known North Macedonian firm Cytrox of infecting the phones of Egyptian dissidents with its Predator spyware. 13/ Important to call out the remarkable investigative work of @jsrailton and the entire team at @citizenlab, who are releasing a deep dive report into one of these cases today and shared information with us that enabled us to identify and share IOCs. https://t.co/WFbE8E7NKM Cytrox is reportedly part of an alliance of firms created to compete against Israel-based NSO Group, the producer of spyware tool Pegasus. Bluehawk CI, an Israeli firm, allegedly posed as a Fox News correspondent and a journalist working for Italian newspaper La Stampa to help the ruler of one of the UAEâ€™s emirates in a litigation, according to a Daily Beast report. Another of the firms targeted by Meta today, Israeli firm Bluehawk-CI, was first identified by The Daily Beast with help from FB security back in April when we found the company posing as Fox News and spying on critics of the UAE's Ras Al Khaimah Emirate. https://t.co/ycrzYik0g1 The seventh target of Metaâ€™s purge was described as an â€œunknown entityâ€ that was accused of deploying â€œmalware toolsâ€ against minority groups in Chinaâ€™s Xinjiang region and Hong Kong as well as Myanmar. The entity, according to Meta, was allegedly involved in â€œdomestic law enforcementâ€ in China. Meta investigators expressed hope that the report will help people better understand â€œthe harms this industry represents worldwideâ€ and called on â€œdemocratic governments to take further steps to help protect people and impose oversight on the sellers of ubiquitous spyware.â€ Gleicher specifically welcomed a recent joint statement from his former colleagues at the White House and Americaâ€™s allies Australia, Denmark, and Norway, who decried electronic surveillance by â€œauthoritarian governments.â€ Before joining Metaâ€™s team, Gleicher worked at the US National Security Council, as did Agranovich. Dvilyanski, the third author of the report, is a former FBI cybersecurity agent.

title: Judicial nominee refuses to say if crimes should be forgiven â€˜in name of social justiceâ€™ (VIDEO)

title: 100+ Marines kicked out of force for defying vaccine mandate
text: Over a hundred US Marines have been discharged for refusing to get vaccinated against Covid-19 as military punishments ramp up under President Joe Bidenâ€™s strict vaccine mandate. The Marine Corps confirmed the discharges on Thursday in a statement to the Marine Corps Times. The 103 soldiers who have been booted from the force so far are expected to receive either an honorable or general discharge. Marine Corps spokesman Maj. Jim Stenger told the magazine that 1,007 vaccine exemptions for medical and administrative reasons were granted, while 2,836 requests for religious exemptions have been rejected so far. It is widely expected that the force, which has yet to grant a single soldier an exemption on religious grounds over Covid-19 vaccination, would turn down nearly 300 remaining applications. Although the Marine Corps was revealed last month to be the least vaccinated US military branch, the overwhelming majority of its personnel â€“ about 95% â€“ have received at least one dose of a Covid-19 vaccine. Active-duty personnel had been given until November 28 to either get vaccinated against the virus or apply for an exemption. The news on the mass dismissal of Marines comes shortly after 27 US Air Force service members â€“ who were described as â€œyounger, lower-ranking personnelâ€ â€“ were revealed to have been discharged this week for refusing to get vaccinated. The terminated Air Force personnel did not seek any exemptions and were officially sanctioned for disobeying orders. The US Navy is expected to follow suit in the near future. As of last week, 5,731 US Navy personnel remained unvaccinated despite a mandate requiring all active-duty sailors to get the shot by the November 28 deadline. It has been reported that as many as 40,000 US military personnel either refused vaccination against Covid-19 or sought an exemption â€“ amounting to roughly 3% of troops.

title: Judge orders search of Alec Baldwinâ€™s phone after shooting

Alexandria Hancock requested a warrant â€œfor the seizure and searchâ€ of Baldwinâ€™s phone, expressing her belief that â€œthere may be evidenceâ€ on the device due to Baldwin using it â€œduring and/or after the commission of the crime.â€ The detective also expressed interest in â€œseveral emails and text messages sent and received regarding the movie production â€˜Rustâ€™ in the course of interviews.â€ The search warrant request was approved by a New Mexico judge on Thursday, who gave police permission to seize the phone at any time of the day between 6am and 10pm. Hutchins was killed on the set of Baldwinâ€™s Western movie â€˜Rustâ€™ in October and director Joel Souza was hospitalized after a prop gun Baldwin was holding discharged. Though the gun was in Baldwinâ€™s hand when it killed Hutchins, the actor insisted in a controversial interview this month that he had never pulled the trigger. â€œThe trigger wasnâ€™t pulled. I didnâ€™t pull the trigger,â€ Baldwin claimed, insisting he would â€œnever point a gun at anyone and pull the trigger at them, never.â€ Baldwin also told ABC News that he did not feel responsible for Hutchinsâ€™ death, saying, â€œSomeone is responsible... but I know it's not me.â€ However, script supervisor Mamie Mitchell claimed in a lawsuit that Baldwin â€œintentionally, without just cause or excuse, cocked and fired the loaded gun even though the upcoming scene to be filmed did not call for the cocking and firing of the firearm.â€ â€œMr. Baldwin chose to play Russian Roulette with a loaded gun without checking it and without having the armorer do so,â€ the lawsuit alleged.

title: US Marines chief reveals biggest risk for his force
text: The US Marine Corps risks being left without the weapons it will need to fight, unless Congress and the Pentagon fund new programs amid a purge of old technology, its commandant has warned. General David Berger warned that, if the Congress and the Pentagon were not â€œwilling to backâ€ his force, the USMC might end up â€œin a bad placeâ€ after it gets rid of â€œlegacy thingsâ€ such as tanks and artillery without receiving new cutting-edge capabilities to replace them. â€œWeâ€™re in that middle ground where weâ€™re rapidly changing,â€ he told an online event hosted by the Center for a New American Security on Tuesday. â€œIf youâ€™re left in a lurch there, thatâ€™s not a good place to be.â€ The generalâ€™s concerns were linked to the Marinesâ€™ new strategy dubbed â€˜USMC Force Design 2030.â€™ Over the past several years, the USMC moved â€œto divest, or get rid of things that may have been useful in the past, but were not as useful going forward.â€ The force discarded what it considered outdated hardware not fitting its new, agile and more expeditionary role. In addition to tanks and artillery and bridging companies, the Marines also got rid of heavy helicopters in preparation of pursuing â€œthe next-generation capabilities for the future,â€ as the USMC put it in May. As soon as 2023, Berger hopes to equip Marines with NMESIS anti-ship missile launchers paired with drone ammunition carriers and Joint Light Tactical Vehicles (JLTV) for greater mobility and firepower. He also wants more radars and F-35 stealth fighters. Currently, however, his most pressing priority is to buy light amphibious warships (LAW) to make his force more mobile. The ships were supposed to be included in the acquisition list for the fiscal year 2022 but were ditched by the Navy because of a budgetary decision. Now, Berger hopes their purchase would be in the fiscal year 2023 budget cycle. â€œIf we donâ€™t do that, then youâ€™ll have the stand-in force thatâ€™s forward without an organic ability to move around,â€ the general said, adding that the force cannot wait â€œthree or four years to assess what our requirement is. We canâ€™t move like that anymore.â€ Outlining the Marinesâ€™ new strategy, Berger suggested sending â€œsmall but lethalâ€ mobile units made up of USMC, Navy and Coast Guard forces on missions â€œbelow the threshold of violenceâ€ in contested areas like the South China Sea. Having these forces would enable the US to â€œassist in identifying and countering malign behavior,â€ the general said in a December 1 report, adding that â€œif armed conflict does erupt, the joint force can attack effectively first and prevent the enemy from doing so.â€

title: Biden predicts 'winter of death' for unvaxxed
text: US President Joe Biden urged all Americans to receive booster shots and warned of a winter full of â€œsevere illness and deathâ€ for those who remain unvaccinated amid the spread of the Omicron variant of Covid-19. â€œIf youâ€™re vaccinated and have your booster shot, youâ€™re protected from severe illness and death,â€ Biden said on Thursday, in brief remarks to the press as he met with his Covid-19 coordination team at the White House. â€œDue to the steps weâ€™ve taken, Omicron has not spread as fast as it could have otherwise done,â€ Biden added, â€œbut itâ€™s here now and itâ€™s spreading and itâ€™s gonna increase.â€ We are looking at a winter of severe illness and death for the unvaccinated. The White House responded to the discovery of the variant â€“ designated Omicron by the World Health Organization in late November â€“ by banning travelers from eight African countries where it was first detected. The ban went into effect on November 29. The first US case of the Omicron contagion was detected two days later in California, in a traveler who returned from South Africa on November 22. As of Wednesday, 36 US states have reported cases of Omicron, which was said to amount to 3% of total infections across the country. Health authorities across the world consider Omicron to be far more transmissible than the Delta variant, blamed for the spike in US coronavirus deaths this year. title: Sex and the City star accused of sexual assault
text: The revival of iconic US TV series Sex and the City has triggered two women who claim they were sexually assaulted by one of the showâ€™s stars to come forward with painful memories they thought they had â€œburied.â€ The return of SATC and its male star Chris Noth â€“ â€˜Mr. Bigâ€™ â€“ to the small screen in And Just Like That has led two women to come forward with vivid memories of being assaulted by the actor. The pair approached The Hollywood Reporter independently over the past several months to share their stories, which despite taking place 11 years apart on opposite sides of the country have a lot in common. â€˜Zoeâ€™, who approached THR in October, opted to â€œtry to go public with who [Noth] isâ€ as the hype was building over the new TV series. Still employed in the entertainment industry, she told the magazine that â€œfor so many years, [she] buriedâ€ the memory of the assault, which took place in Los Angeles in 2004 as Zoe was beginning her career in the industry. While Noth, who was represented by the firm she worked for, was â€œkind of flirty,â€ she thought nothing of it, given his celebrity at the time of â€œpeak SATC.â€ It was only when she stopped by his apartment to return a book he had lent her that things went dreadfully wrong, with a surprise kiss quickly devolving into sexual assault. A friend who took her to the hospital and a former boss she allegedly spoke to both corroborated her story, and Zoe noted that she did not want to end her life like her mother, diagnosed with cancer in 2018 and â€œhauntedâ€ by a sexual assault she had kept quiet for years. â€˜Lilyâ€™, who came forward in August, was allegedly approached by Noth while working at a New York nightclub, invited to a restaurant shortly before closing time and later shepherded to the actorâ€™s apartment. After â€œhe kept tryingâ€ to make out with Lily against her will, he allegedly raped her in a similar fashion to his reported assault on â€˜Zoeâ€™. She shared the incident with a friend shortly thereafter, and Noth allegedly sent multiple text messages seemingly attempting to gauge her response to (and minimize) the assault. Contacted by the magazine, Noth addressed both womenâ€™s claims by declaring the accusations â€œcategorically false,â€ noting that whether â€œ30 years ago or 30 days ago, no always means noâ€ and that the â€œencounters were consensual.â€ â€œItâ€™s difficult not to question the timing of these stories coming out,â€ he said.

title: US blacklists Chinese firms over â€˜brain-control weaponryâ€™
text: The US Treasury has blacklisted 34 Chinese companies and research institutes, with Washington accusing one of the named institutes of developing â€œbrain-control weaponry.â€ The Chinese institutes and firms were added to the departmentâ€™s â€˜Entity Listâ€™ on Wednesday, joining more than 260 other Chinese businesses â€“ including smartphone giant Huawei â€“ already on the list. Placement on the list forbids these firms from buying technology from the US without express permission from Washington. Among the entities listed are the Chinese Academy of Military Medical Sciences (AMMS) and 11 of its research institutes. In an entry to the Federal Register published Thursday, the Biden administration claimed that these institutes â€œuse biotechnology processes to support [the] Chinese military,â€ and have developed â€œpurported brain-control weaponry.â€ â€œThe scientific pursuit of biotechnology and medical innovation can save lives. Unfortunately, the PRC is choosing to use these technologies to pursue control over its people and its repression of members of ethnic and religious minority groups,â€ Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo wrote in a statement, referring to the Peopleâ€™s Republic of Chinaâ€™s alleged human rights abuses against Uighur Muslims in the Chinese province of Xinjiang. Four other companies were added to the list â€œfor their support of Chinaâ€™s military modernization,â€ while five additional firms were added for allegedly trying to acquire US technology to help the Chinese military. The Federal Register entry did not elaborate further on the alleged Chinese â€œbrain-control weaponry,â€ nor did it specify which of the AMMSâ€™ institutes was behind this supposed weaponry. The Biden administration has largely continued former President Donald Trumpâ€™s antagonistic stance toward Beijing. While Biden has not imposed any fresh tariffs on Chinese goods, he has not removed those put in place by Trump. In addition, the Biden administration continues to target the Chinese technology sector with sanctions, expanding a Trump-era ban on American investments in companies working with the Chinese military, and weighing sanctions on the countryâ€™s largest semiconductor manufacturer.

title: â€˜My phone is a brickâ€™: Russians scramble for information as data blocked
text: On Friday, a group of children dressed in red took to the stage on Field of Wonders, a game show which has been broadcast on Russian television since late Soviet times. â€œWe donâ€™t want it, we donâ€™t want it,â€ the children sang cheerfully. â€œWe donâ€™t sit, we donâ€™t sit on your internet.â€ The song finished optimistically, suggesting that instead of doomscrolling, â€œitâ€™s much more fun to meet your friends nearby!â€ While it might well be good for youngsters to play outside every once in a while, given the ongoing war with Ukraine, the song was perhaps also aimed at older viewers. While internet outages have been happening periodically over the past year in the border regions, where fighting has spilled over from Ukraine, this month, major cities such as Moscow and Saint Petersburg have experienced blackouts as well. Observers say signs point to the Kremlin tightening its grip on cyberspace. The outages only seem to affect mobile data, leaving Wi-Fi functional, and parts of the capital, especially the outskirts, have been spared the shutdown. But going offline has disrupted everyday life. People say it has become impossible to message friends or colleagues on the go, or to check your phone for directions. â€œWe practically have no mobile internet now,â€ Diana, a St Petersburg teacher in her mid-30s, told Al Jazeera. â€œThat means you canâ€™t use maps, apps, or anything. And in Moscow, you canâ€™t even call from downtown. The phoneâ€™s just turned into a brick. Yes, and you can only pay for anything in cash. In short, you feel like youâ€™re 20 years in the past.â€ Earlier this month, the newspaper Kommersant estimated that Moscowâ€™s economy lost 3-5 billion rubles ($36m-$65m) in just five days of shutdown in the city. Authorities have stated that the outages, which began in central Moscow but have now spread elsewhere in the country, are necessary for â€œsecurityâ€ in light of recent Ukrainian drone attacks. â€œThat reasoning is not particularly convincing,â€ Anastasiya Zhyrmont, policy manager for Eastern Europe and Central Asia at the digital rights group Access Now, told Al Jazeera. â€œDisrupting civilian internet access is a blunt instrument and is widely seen by experts as ineffective against the kind of threats being cited.â€ Instead, Zhyrmont suggested, a more plausible explanation is that these blackouts are being used to test the governmentâ€™s so-called â€œwhitelistâ€ of approved websites, through which only approved services or platforms will remain accessible while everything else is blocked. The blackouts have proven deeply unpopular, even among those usually supportive of the Kremlin. Vyacheslav Gladkov, governor of the embattled Belgorod region bordering Ukraine, which has come under artillery fire and drone attacks, has sharply criticised the internet outages and called for Roskomnadzor â€“ Russiaâ€™s cyber-censorship agency â€“ to â€œbe put on trialâ€. â€œWho will answer for the deaths of people who were unable to get information about drones because mobile internet was shut down? Did the people who did this use their heads at all?â€ he asked in a live broadcast last week. The Russian government has been gradually imposing online censorship since the 2010s, tasking Roskomnadzor with blacklisting websites allegedly promoting drug abuse, suicide and child abuse. However, in practice, this has meant blocking pages offering help and advice for people struggling with these issues, and even Wikipedia articles about them. In 2019, the â€œsovereign internetâ€ law was passed, requiring internet providers to install state-controlled monitoring equipment in their facilities. This allowed real-time filtering, surveillance and the selective blocking of online traffic. â€œThe â€˜sovereign internetâ€™ refers to a model of internet governance where a state seeks to tightly control digital infrastructure, data flows, and online content within its borders,â€ Zhyrmont said. â€œBy restricting access to external platforms, the state reduces exposure to independent reporting and alternative viewpoints, reinforcing its ability to shape public narratives for propaganda purposes.â€ At the same time, she said, internet traffic under controlled infrastructure enables surveillance capabilities, making it easier to monitor communications and identify dissent. â€œThis creates a tightly managed digital space where access to information is filtered, controlled and, when necessary, suppressed. In that sense, the â€˜sovereign internetâ€™ is not just about digital autonomy â€“ it is about information control, enabling propaganda, surveillance and censorship at scale.â€ Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, cyber-censorship in Russia has rapidly accelerated. Popular social media such as Facebook, Instagram, the gaming platform Roblox, and the messaging app WhatsApp have been blocked on the grounds that they are used to spread â€œfake newsâ€ about the war in Ukraine. Another technique is â€œthrottlingâ€ â€“ not blocking websites outright, but deliberately slowing them to the point the user is frustrated and gives up. When YouTube was throttled in 2024, authorities blamed the websiteâ€™s slow speed on Googleâ€™s servers, a claim the company denied. Russian authorities have also taken steps to pressure app stores to remove VPNs (virtual private networks), which can be used to bypass restrictions. Although more than one-third of Russians use VPNs, according to Levada, an independent polling organisation, the majority, especially the elderly, still do not. â€œAt the request of Roskomnadzor, Apple quietly removed dozens of VPN services from the Russian app store, and independent monitoring found nearly 100 apps effectively unavailable,â€ said Zhyrmont. â€œOn the technical side, Russian filtering infrastructure can detect and block many popular VPN protocols.â€ Then, Russians lost access to Telegram last week, with access only restored on Sunday after Roskomnadzorâ€™s attempts to block the popular app reportedly ran into technical difficulties, something the agency has denied. Roskomnadzor did not respond to requests for comment from Al Jazeera. â€œIn my opinion, Telegram is currently the most important source of communication and information for Russians,â€ Russian social democrat politician Nikolai Kavkazsky told Al Jazeera. â€œFor me, the most obvious reason is that the authorities want to restrict free communication and expression among Russians, men and women, even though the Russian Constitution and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights guarantee these rights â€¦ They also want to sever the connection between [the opposition-minded diaspora] and those who remained.â€ The founder and CEO of Telegram, St Petersburg-born Pavel Durov, who was arrested in France last year on charges of failing to prevent illegal activity on the app, has long been at odds with the Russian government over freedom of speech. In 2014, he sold his stake in the hugely popular social media platform he founded, VKontakte (VK), and fled Russia. Since then, the authorities have claimed his Telegram app is a liability exploited by NATO and Ukrainian intelligence. Amid the Russia-Ukraine war, Telegram has been used as a communications tool by both sidesâ€™ forces, but there have been reports from independent Russian media that Russian soldiers are being ordered to delete the app. Failing to do so can get them reassigned to the dreaded Storm-Z battalions, deployed on suicidal charges towards enemy lines. In February, Russia opened a criminal investigation into Durov for facilitating â€œterrorismâ€. Around the same time, Telegram started being throttled, in preparation for a full block, which is set to come into effect on April 1. Dima, a Moscow-based political consultant in his early 30s who did not wish to give his full name for fear of repercussions, played down the disruption. â€œTelegram worked even without a VPN, but it only loaded text,â€ he told Al Jazeera. â€œBasically, commoners and old-timers who didnâ€™t have a VPN have been deprived of Telegram. Telegram has become elitist. Otherwise, everythingâ€™s the same.â€ To replace Telegram and other social media platforms, the Russian government has been heavily promoting an alternative cyberspace. After YouTube was throttled, a number of Russian imitators appeared, nicknamed â€œYouTube killers,â€ such as Nuum and Platforma, but have struggled to win popularity. Only the more established VK Video, linked to the social network of the same name, has roughly comparable viewership with YouTube. But the most talked-about new app is Max. More than a Telegram alternative for chatting and sharing news and media, Max is designed to be a super app, catering to a wider range of citizensâ€™ needs. â€œI installed it on my second phone,â€ said Diana, the teacher. â€œWe have no options now â€“ if you want to make a doctorâ€™s appointment or pay taxes, for example, you have to get it through Max. The code for accessing government services doesnâ€™t come anywhere else.â€ Diana hasnâ€™t installed Max on her primary phone for fear that, besides being a way of sharing funny cat videos, the app is a mass surveillance tool. According to Zhyrmont, â€œMax does not merely record user messages or metadata. â€œMAX can report your real-time movements â€“ a tool that, in repressive conditions, can expose attendance at protests, political gatherings, or simply trace your personal contacts and mobility,â€ she said. Max also harvests user data: age, gender, links to other accounts, and even search history, exposing the user to fines and other penalties for looking up what the authorities vaguely consider â€œextremistâ€ content â€“ for instance, the so-called â€œinternational LGBTQ movementâ€. â€œThe app is reportedly capable of more invasive operations: silently activating the microphone, camera or screen-recording, even when the user believes the app is idle,â€ Zhyrmont added. Criticism of Russiaâ€™s online restrictions has come from all sides of the political spectrum, from oppositionists like Kavkazsky to hawkish war-supporting bloggers, for whom Telegram has become a major platform. Over the past month, authorities have suppressed protests against Telegram restrictions across the country. â€œThe youth have had all their popular services blocked, and whereas before, when [SWIFT] payment systems were blocked, that could be blamed on Western sanctions, now itâ€™s our Russian state taking this away,â€ observed 39-year-old St Petersburg resident Kirill F. â€œThe younger generation only sees violations of their personal boundaries.â€ Zhyrmont believes that while state-approved services will resume to quell public frustration, the overall trajectory points to a normalisation of internet shutdowns where the government can control access during â€œsensitive movementsâ€. Nevertheless, a total ban on VPNs is unlikely, so that select organisations can retain access for â€œlegitimate useâ€. â€œThat said, given the broader trajectory of digital control in recent years, nothing can be completely ruled out,â€ she said.
